table.brief: Bill of materials: Part number (like RC0402FR-0710KL) / Description (long) / Qty / Unit price / Supplier

understanding.purpose: A bill of materials for identifying, sourcing and costing the parts needed for a prototype controller board.
understanding.reading: Readers scan each row from part number and description to quantity, unit price and supplier, and compare quantities and prices down their columns. Long descriptions can set row height, leaving room for other cells to wrap without necessarily making the row taller.
groups: Part number and description identify the component and its specifications.
Quantity and unit price are compact numerical fields used together for purchasing and cost comparison.
Supplier belongs with the purchasing fields and identifies where to source each part.
keep_intact: Part numbers and other component identifiers, so they can be copied and distinguished reliably.
Quantities and individual price values, so numbers and currency remain easy to compare.
Supplier names where possible, especially when they are used as search terms.
may_wrap: Descriptions at natural word and punctuation boundaries, while keeping individual specifications legible.
Headers at word boundaries where needed.
Supplier names at natural boundaries when the available width requires it.

preferred.name: r2A
preferred.note: Give descriptions 12px more than r1A to improve specification wrapping and row rhythm while preserving intact identifiers, prices and suppliers. This accepts a little more horizontal scrolling.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Keep part numbers, prices and supplier names intact while reducing description width and allowing the price header to wrap. This tests a smaller horizontal footprint with taller descriptions but no forced splits in supplier names.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Give the description its 128px minimum for the longest unbreakable word. The first three columns total 361px, putting quantity almost entirely in the first viewport without the word split seen in r1C.

acceptable.name: r2C
acceptable.note: Test a middle ground between r1A and r1B: recover some description space, retain the single-line price header, and reduce horizontal travel slightly compared with r1A.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Give descriptions more room than r2A to improve phrase grouping and potentially reduce row heights. Readers must scroll to reach all purchasing fields, but the initial view emphasizes component identification.

acceptable.name: r3C
acceptable.note: Widen the description modestly from r2A and reduce unit price to its 59px text requirement plus padding. This tests a more readable description while keeping price values intact and limiting the increase in total width.

bad.name: r1C
bad.note: Bring the complete Qty column into the initial 359px viewport while keeping identifiers, price values and suppliers intact. The narrower description trades taller rows for immediate access to quantities.
bad.why: The description is narrow enough to strand the comma after “Microcontroller” on the next line, and the resulting six-line cell makes that row especially tall.

bad.name: r3A
bad.note: Use the full 359px viewport for part number, description and quantity. This preserves identifiers and makes quantities visible at first sight, while accepting dense description wrapping and scrolling for price and supplier.
bad.why: It duplicates r1C’s widths and has the same stranded punctuation and six-line description.

rationale: r2A keeps part numbers intact and gives descriptions enough room to read in three or four lines, so rows remain easy to follow. Its headers stay on one line, while the initial viewport shows the part number and nearly all of the description; quantity, price and supplier require horizontal scrolling. The narrower alternatives save some scrolling but make descriptions substantially taller, while r3B gains a shorter table at the cost of cutting descriptions at the viewport edge.

general: Preserve identifiers and meaningful words, and give prose enough width for rows to read as units.
Judge horizontal scrolling alongside vertical density and what a reader can see at the initial viewport.
Keep related headers and values readable without giving every column equal width.
specific: The long part numbers and supplier names set substantial minimum widths for this BOM.
A modest increase in description width from r2C to r2A substantially reduces wrapping, while keeping the description nearly within the initial viewport.

tradeoffs: r2B exposes quantity in the initial viewport and requires less horizontal scrolling, but its descriptions are much taller. r3B makes the rows shorter, but every description extends beyond the initial viewport and the remaining columns are farther away.
uncertain: The ranges are conservative estimates around r2A, not browser-tested equivalence boundaries; wrapping can change at individual pixel thresholds. A designer who values seeing quantity immediately could reasonably prefer r2B.

critique.good: Part numbers, price values and supplier names remain intact. The description wraps into readable phrases, and the compact rows preserve useful visual connections across the table.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows the identifying columns but cuts through Qty; unit price and supplier require substantial horizontal scrolling. The reader must scroll to complete the purchasing information for each row.
critique.cause: The 186px part-number and 160px description columns consume 346px before Qty begins. The 639px total extends 279px beyond the viewport.

critique.good: Part numbers and quantities remain intact, and the narrower total reduces horizontal travel. More of Qty appears at the viewport edge.
critique.problems: Descriptions are noticeably taller and more fragmented, while supplier names split within words. The wrapped price header adds height to every header cell, and the purchasing fields still require scrolling.
critique.cause: Reducing Description to 145px increases wrapping; the 105px Supplier column cannot contain its longest unbreakable name. Unit price at 80px is too narrow for its header on one line.

critique.good: All five columns appear at once, making their relationship visible without horizontal scrolling. Qty remains compact and legible.
critique.problems: Part numbers, descriptions, prices and suppliers break within words or values. The narrow columns create very tall rows and a fragmented header, making identification and price comparison difficult.
critique.cause: The 100px part-number, 105px description, 54px price and 53px supplier widths leave too little text space after padding. Fitting the entire table into 360px forces splits across essential fields.

critique.good: Part numbers, prices and supplier names remain intact. The description has enough room for comparatively natural wrapping, and the single-line headers give the table a clear, compact rhythm.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through the quantity column, so readers cannot comfortably scan the complete identification and quantity fields together. Price and supplier require horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 186px part-number and 153px description columns consume 339px before the 47px quantity column begins. The full table is 632px wide.

critique.good: Part numbers and supplier names remain intact, and more of the quantity column appears in the first viewport than in r1A. The narrower table reduces horizontal travel slightly.
critique.problems: Descriptions wrap more often, producing a taller table and a less even rhythm. The price header wraps, increasing the header height, while the purchasing columns still require scrolling.
critique.cause: Reducing the description to 139px increases wrapping; reducing unit price to 80px leaves only 59px for text, too little for its one-line header.

critique.good: Quantity fits almost entirely in the first viewport, and the unit-price header has room to stay on one line. Part numbers and supplier names remain intact.
critique.problems: The narrow description breaks a word and creates a six-line cell. The resulting tall rows make specifications harder to scan, while price and supplier still require scrolling.
critique.cause: At 126px, the description has only 105px of text space, less than its 107px longest unbreakable word. The 186px part-number width leaves little room for description and quantity within the viewport.

critique.good: The part numbers remain intact, and the description has enough room for relatively coherent phrases. Its shorter rows make it easier to follow each component across the table.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the quantity column, so even the quantity cannot be read comfortably without scrolling. Price and supplier are farther to the right.
critique.cause: The 186px part-number column and 165px description column consume 351px before the 47px quantity column begins. The purchasing columns add substantial horizontal overflow.

critique.good: Part numbers remain intact, and the complete quantity column fits in the initial viewport. The purchasing fields are closer at hand than in the other designs.
critique.problems: Descriptions form narrow, uneven blocks. The microcontroller description reaches six lines, and specifications such as Cortex-M3 and SOT-23-6 break across lines, making rows tall and harder to scan.
critique.cause: The 128px description column leaves only 107px for text. That width fits the longest unbreakable word but forces frequent wrapping at punctuation and spaces.

critique.good: It preserves intact part numbers and gives descriptions more breathing room than r2B; the microcontroller description occupies five rather than six lines.
critique.problems: The viewport cuts through quantity, while descriptions still wrap into tall blocks with awkward breaks in specifications. It gives up r2B's complete view of quantity without achieving r2A's more compact rows.
critique.cause: At 145px, the description column is still narrow, but the first two columns already total 331px, leaving only 29px of the 47px quantity column within the viewport.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r1C.why: Part numbers and quantities fit in the viewport, but the narrow description column produces tall rows and strands punctuation after “Microcontroller.” Price and supplier require scrolling.

r2A.why: The wider description column gives the text a more comfortable rhythm and keeps part numbers intact. Quantity falls mostly beyond the viewport, so comparing it with the descriptions requires scrolling.

ref_auto.why: Part numbers and quantities are visible, and descriptions wrap mostly at sensible points. The rows are tall, the price header wraps, and price and supplier require scrolling.

ref_equal.why: All five columns fit, but part numbers, descriptions, supplier names and some prices split across lines. The resulting tall rows are difficult to scan and compare.

r1B.why: Part numbers remain intact and descriptions wrap reasonably, though quantity sits at the viewport edge and the remaining columns require scrolling.

r2B.why: Part numbers and quantities fit in the viewport, while descriptions wrap mostly at natural boundaries. Price and supplier still require scrolling, but the visible columns retain a clear hierarchy.

raw.unsure: The supplied images cut off most of the horizontally scrolled area, so the widths and readability of price and supplier cannot be fully assessed. B offers more comfortable descriptions, but its quantity column is largely outside the initial viewport.

r1B.why: Part numbers stay intact and descriptions are readable, but the quantity column is cut by the viewport edge and the tall header suggests wrapping in columns farther right.

r2A.why: The wider description column gives the rows a more comfortable rhythm and keeps part numbers intact, but quantity falls beyond the initial viewport along with price and supplier.

r1C.why: Part numbers and quantities are visible together, but the narrow description column strands the comma after “Microcontroller” and makes several rows tall.

ref_auto.why: Part numbers and quantities fit in the viewport, and descriptions generally wrap at sensible points. The tall header and partially visible price column weaken the hierarchy.

r2B.why: Part numbers and quantities are visible together, with descriptions wrapping mostly at sensible points and a compact, clear header. Price and supplier require horizontal scrolling.

ref_equal.why: Although all columns fit, headers, part numbers, descriptions, prices and supplier names split across lines, making rows difficult to scan and values difficult to read.

raw.unsure: The supplied images cut off the right side of layouts A–E, so I cannot assess the full widths or wrapping of their price and supplier columns or compare their total scrolling distances.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
